ab_answer: Milpa Gardens is a free garden planner that gives advice only where it can back it up. Each piece of advice comes from a rule, and each rule says why it works and how strong the evidence is.

ab_who_p: Milpa is a small independent project run by one maintainer. Much of its code and writing was drafted with an AI language model. A person reviews each change before it goes live, and only a person can mark a source as read.
ab_who_words: From the maintainer: “I’m new to gardening, and building Milpa is how I’m learning it. I started it because I couldn’t find one place online that gathered what a gardener needs, whether it’s a first bed or a long-tended plot. My background is in delivering software systems, turning complex requirements into tools experts can rely on, and I’ve brought that same care here. I read the sources behind Milpa’s claims one by one and check that each says what we say it does, and a claim I haven’t read yet is marked that way. Every source I read teaches me a little more about gardening, and what I learn goes straight back into Milpa.”
ab_why_p: A lot of garden advice comes with no reason attached, and some of it is folklore. Milpa plans your beds, dates your sowing from your own frost dates and keeps a record of what grew where. Each step shows the reason behind it, so you can judge it for yourself.

cp_grades_html: Every rule carries one of {n} grades, from “{top}” down to “{bottom}”, and the file spells each grade out in those words. A rule is graded “{top}”, “{b}” or “{c}” only if it can state its mechanism in one sentence; a claim that only correlates is downgraded or dropped. The file also holds the refuted tier, {refuted} folk claims this corpus checked and rejected, because a correction is worth as much as a rule.
cp_license_html: The corpus is offered under {license}. You can use it, build on it and ship it, as long as you credit it and pass on the same freedom. Share-alike is deliberate. cp_what: One entry per rule, in machine-readable form: the claim, the named mechanism, the evidence grade, whether the sources have been verified by a person, the sources themselves and, when the file is built from a full clone of the history, the dated record of every change that rule has been through. A stable identifier on each rule lets you cite one and find it again. The file names the exact commit it was built from, so two people who download it can tell whether they are looking at the same corpus.

fe_answer: You can point a class at this site because every claim on it carries an evidence grade, names the mechanism it works by, links the sources it rests on, and says plainly which of its own numbers it does not stand behind. Where it does not know, it says so.
fe_cite_html: Every rule, folklore and plant page carries a “{cite}” block with a ready citation. For a rule or belief, the evidence grade is part of it. Please keep the grade when you quote a claim (“Milpa Gardens rates this {grade}”), so your students see how sure it is, the same way you do.
fe_climate_html: Its climate data is strongest in the United States. Frost dates there come from NOAA’s {start} to {end} climate normals at {stations} weather stations, and hardiness zones from the USDA {vintage} Plant Hardiness Zone Map, made with the PRISM Climate Group at Oregon State University. {abroad} The model is ERA5, and its estimates are graded {grade}.{local} {link} shows where each frost date comes from and how sure it is.
fe_contact_html: Questions, corrections and reports of a wrong claim go to {mail}. Every rule and folklore page also has a link for reporting a problem with that claim. The {sources} are listed by publisher, with how many a person has read.
fe_corpus_html: You can also take the whole graded set with you: the {link} is every rule, its mechanism, its grade and its sources in one file, under a share-alike license. You can hand it to a class or check it yourself.
fe_desc: Why a class can use Milpa Gardens: what its evidence grades mean, what verified and unverified mean, what it refuses to do, and how to cite a claim with its grade.
fe_grade_p: Every rule carries one of {n} grades. The word is the grade, and the sentence is what it commits to. These counts are read from the live corpus of {rules} rules, so they show the real distribution.
fe_lede: Milpa Gardens is a garden-planning corpus of rules, folklore checked against the literature, and species records. A person reads each source before a claim built on it is marked verified, and approves every change to the rules. The text was drafted with an LLM and then held to rules that most gardening content, AI-written or not, is not held to. This page sets out those rules in plain language, so you can judge whether it belongs in front of students.

fe_mechanism_html: A rule is graded “{a}”, “{b}” or “{c}” only if it can state its mechanism in one sentence, and the top two never lean on the word “helps”. A claim that only correlates, or works by a mechanism nobody can name, is downgraded or dropped. Sounding right does not earn it the top grade.

fe_noev_one_html: One rule is marked as having no evidence at all, which is a person’s judgment that the literature is silent.
fe_not_html: It is not a substitute for your local extension office or a soil test, and it is not safety or medical advice. A toxicity note is a general caution, not a poison-control reference. {climate} It plans gardens from evidence, and it does not replace an agronomist.
fe_partners_html: If your school, extension office or community garden starts using Milpa before the organization plan opens, write to {mail}. You’ll get that plan free the day it opens, and a say in what it includes.
fe_refuse_chart: It publishes no companion-planting chart. Folk claims that fail a check against the literature, pairings among them, are marked refuted and kept as corrections: {rules} and {beliefs}.
fe_refuse_fit: It never plans a planting that does not fit the space you gave it. A plant team too big for your bed is grayed out with the reason and the nearest one that does fit, never hidden and never swapped without telling you.
fe_refuse_fixer_html: It recommends no woody nitrogen-fixer without checking the state noxious-weed list first. Several are invasive, so “fixes nitrogen” alone is no reason to plant one.
fe_refuse_gdd: It invents no growing-degree-day maturity by analogy. A crop with no real GDD model in the literature does not get one, because guessing it from a similar plant would be fabrication.
fe_refuse_lapse: It applies no elevation temperature correction to frost. On the clear, still nights when frost forms, cold air pools in low ground, so the textbook lapse-rate adjustment predicts the opposite of what happens. The corpus leaves it out.
fe_refuse_npk_html: It gives no fertilizer NPK numbers without a soil test. Asked what to feed a bed, it says “get a soil test” and stops. It will not guess a number without one.
fe_refuse_p: Each of these is enforced, and each has a reason a student can check.
fe_soft_html: Numbers get the same treatment at the field level. A species’ size, spacing or timing figure is marked estimated or contested when it is not from a firm source. All {n} of them are listed on {link}.
fe_unv_none: None of the rules are unverified.

fe_verified_html: Verified means a person read a real source, named in the rule’s sources, and confirmed the claim, or that the rule is true by arithmetic or geometry. {counts} Unverified means an LLM asserted it from general knowledge and no person has checked a source. It is labeled as such and never presented as fact. {unverified}{none} Promoting a claim from unverified to verified requires a person reading the source, and the model is never allowed to promote its own work.

Nothing else in a US answer is modeled or averaged. It is the same committed table behind every location page on this site, read a second way. hp_loc_world: Outside the US, a weather model estimates your frost dates and zone, and far from any of its readings only daylength works. Where a weather station near your garden has a long daily record, its own frost dates take the model’s place, and the app names it. The coverage page shows what works where. If you know your own frost dates, anywhere, enter them under your place on the Plan, or on the Calendar’s climate card, and your plans go by yours.
hp_offline_a: Yes. Open it once with a connection and it keeps working without one.
hp_remind_a: Yes, without nagging. On the day you pick, “Your week” sums up the next seven days by what you do across all your beds. A heads-up comes only on the days that can’t wait: a frost date, a hot or dry stretch starting, a last call to sow. Choose how often on the Calendar, under “Add to your calendar, or set reminders.”
hp_remind_bell: In the app, the bell at the top shows the same notices. Its number counts the ones from the last week you haven’t opened; tap one to see it on the Calendar. Which ones you’ve read is kept on this device.
hp_remind_how: In Chrome or Edge on Android or a computer, Milpa installed as an app can remind you even while it’s closed. On an iPhone or iPad, use “Add to calendar” instead: your calendar app’s alarms remind you, at the pace you chose.

st_answer_html: In the US, type your ZIP code; anywhere else, your city’s name. The tool counts the days from today to your first fall freeze, using the odds from the nearest NOAA station, or, for a city abroad, from a weather station near it or a weather model. Then it sorts the crops by whether they can still finish if you sow now: the ones that beat even an early freeze, the gambles, and the ones that have run out of season. A hardy crop, one that stands a light frost, is counted to the first hard freeze instead, a night of about 28 °F (-2 °C). Where frost sets the season and the months here are too cool for a crop, or a late sowing would ripen into cooler months, it says so beside the crop. Where frost is rare, it lists the crops in season now.

st_why_html: Every crop matures across a range of days: a radish in 22 to 30, a butternut in 90 to 110. This tool counts the fast end plus a week of slack, because that’s the best case for a late sowing, with good soil, a warm autumn and no setbacks. It measures that against your first freeze, which is also a range of dates. Half of years freeze by the median date, and 1 year in 10 the freeze comes earlier. A crop that only clears the median loses to an early freeze in some years, so the safe deadline is the 1-in-10 date.
st_wont: It won’t call a weather service, make up a maturity for a crop that has no recorded one, or promise a harvest. Days to maturity shift with soil, weather and variety, and a first-freeze date is odds. It’s a timing guide built from records that shows which crops are worth the gamble.

Where a city has frost dates, they are odds, with a safer date beside each. Where frost is rare or comes only in some winters, its page says so and lists what to sow when.
wc_lede_station: Where a weather station stands near a city, whether frost is rare or comes in some or most winters is that station’s own count, and the city’s page names it.
wc_lede_undated_html: Frost dates for {cities} in {country}, worked out from a weather model’s daily lows and graded {grade}. Where a city has frost dates, they are odds, with a safer date beside each. Where frost is rare or comes only in some winters, its page says so and lists what to sow when.
wc_map: See every city in {country} on the coverage map
wc_more_p: These cities have no page of their own. The planner answers for each one: tap a city to see its frost dates and what to sow.
wc_rungs: Where the frost dates of the {cities} below come from, each marked the same way beside it.
wc_rungs_one: Where this city’s frost dates come from, marked the same way beside it below.
wn_abroad_p: A garden placed outside the US starts in meters and degrees Celsius, and so does a visit from a world city’s frost page. A garden near a border reads its own country’s weather data, a garden in Mexico gets a route to an accredited soil lab, and where no weather data reaches, three seasons of frosts you log give your garden frost dates of its own.
wn_answer: The latest changes to Milpa, newest first.
wn_answers_city_h: Answers knows cities outside the US
wn_answers_city_p: Outside the US, type the name of a city of 100,000 people or more, and Answers works out its frost dates and what to plant. In the US, your ZIP code does it. When two cities share a name, it asks which one you mean.
wn_app_faster_h: The app opens faster on a phone
wn_app_faster_p: A first visit used to fetch about a hundred separate pieces of code before the app was ready. Now it’s four, with a tenth less code to download, so the first screen comes up sooner on a slow connection.
wn_arch_answer_html: Changes to Milpa from {first} to {last}, by month, newest first. The latest ones are on {link}.
wn_arch_desc: Earlier changes to Milpa Gardens, month by month and newest first, each in plain words with its date.
wn_archive_h: Big changes first, and an archive for the rest
wn_archive_p: What’s new now opens with the biggest recent changes and lists every recent change below them. Older ones move to an archive, month by month, so nothing drops off the site. The changes from late September and early October that had already left this page are back there too.
wn_autumn_weeks_p: Mark a job “Not this year” to set it aside, see the fall jobs as they come, and record the variety you grew. The app also asks your browser to keep your garden’s records safe from clearing.
wn_backup_h: A daily backup of your account
wn_backup_p: Once a day, Milpa saves an encrypted copy of the account database, so a fault on our side can’t lose your garden. Each copy is deleted after 30 days, and the privacy page says where it is kept.
wn_bean_heat_h: Beans wait out the hottest weeks
wn_bean_heat_p: Beans drop their flowers when they bloom in summer heat, so the Calendar no longer suggests a bean sowing that would come ready in a month whose days usually reach 90 °F (32 °C). Where summers run that hot, bean sowings pause in spring and pick up again in late summer for a fall crop, the way lettuce and spinach already wait out the heat.
wn_bed_rename_p: Give a bed a new name in the Plan and it keeps its plans and its place. Before, saving left a copy under the old name on the same spot, so the garden counted one bed too many.
wn_bell_h: A bell for your garden’s news
wn_bell_once_h: The bell tells you about a sowing once
wn_bell_once_p: Where frost is rare, a sowing window can stay open for months, and the bell showed that sowing as new every morning until you logged it. A day’s notice now tells you once, on the day the window opens, and once more a week before a window closes. Your week still lists every sowing open that week, as the Calendar’s week does.
wn_bell_p: A bell at the top of the app now gathers your garden’s notices: “Your week” and its heads-ups. The number on it counts the ones from the last week you haven’t opened. Tap one to see it on the Calendar, or mark them all read. Which ones you’ve read stays on your device.
wn_calendar_plan_h: Next year’s plan on the Calendar
wn_calendar_plan_p: Once you accept next year’s plan for a bed, the Calendar’s month and year views date its jobs. A crop you log on a planned bed keeps its own picking window and re-sowings, and a job names the crop you swapped in.
wn_climate_reading_h: Your climate card says it’s still reading, never “not covered”
wn_climate_reading_p: On a slow connection the climate card could say, for a moment, that your place had no hardiness zone and wasn’t covered, before your real frost dates arrived. Now it says it’s reading your climate until they do.
wn_compare_p: We read every planner on the comparison page against its own pages again. Several lines changed, including what other apps now do better, and one claim we had overstated is softened. From now on the page is re-checked every two months.
wn_coverage_map_h: Where Milpa works: a map you can use
wn_coverage_map_p: The map on the page about where Milpa works is rebuilt. The world is shaded by how many of each country’s cities read a weather station’s own frost dates, with no crowd of dots until you zoom in. Search for a country, a city or a US state, or tap a country, and the map glides there, outlines it in detail and names its cities. On a big screen the map can fill the window, the mouse wheel and the keyboard both work, and the address keeps the view so you can share it. The US shows its NOAA weather stations once you reach a state.
wn_coverage_plain_p: The page on where Milpa works is short and plain. One table shows each source of frost dates, where it reaches, how sure it is and how many places it covers, and one line sums up the rest of what Milpa knows. The map fills a phone’s width, outlines each country, shades the ground the weather model reads and draws the US as its NOAA weather stations. City pages abroad still say where their dates come from and how sure they are, in fewer words.
wn_coverage_zip_h: Where Milpa works: your ZIP code on the map
wn_coverage_zip_p: Type a US ZIP code into the map’s search and it shows the weather station that answers there. The card names the station, how far it is and how sure that makes the dates, with a dashed line to it on the map; tap anywhere in the US for the same answer. Alaska, Hawaii and the territories are frames of their own now, a list names every place in view, and two cities on one spot both get their door.
wn_december_sowing_h: Hardy crops dated before a January frost
wn_december_sowing_p: Where the last frost comes early in January, cabbage and other hardy crops are now dated three weeks before that frost, in December, as the rule says. That’s much of southern California, Florida and Arizona. They used to wait until after the last frost. Answers and the Calendar give the same day.
wn_delete_device_h: Deleting your account clears this device too
wn_delete_device_p: Deleting your account also removes its copy from this device: its gardens, plants, seed box and photos. The gardens you made without signing in stay. Account also has “Sign out of every device”, for a password that may have leaked.
wn_desc: The latest changes to Milpa Gardens, newest first, in plain words with their dates.
wn_doors_bands_h: The front page shows the whole season
wn_doors_bands_p: Under its doors, the front page shows what Milpa works out for each part of the season. Before you plant, it gives the frost odds for Minneapolis from a NOAA weather station. While it grows, it lists a week of jobs in a sample garden in Houston and answers one problem, blossom-end rot, with how sure the answer is. For keeping track, it shows lines from the example garden’s diary from this time last year. For a tip you’ve heard, it gives the tip of the day with its verdict and the source behind it. Each band ends at its own doors.
wn_doors_trail_h: Every answer ends with a next step
wn_doors_trail_p: Every answer in the app and every page on the site now ends with one clear next step and two more doors. Each carries what you were looking at: a plant page asks when to plant it where you are, a frost page offers what can go in now, the symptom finder leads on to that crop’s planting date. The frost tools have one home, the ZIP-or-city lookup on the frost page’s first screen. And a plant Milpa warns against, like autumn olive, is never offered a planting date.
wn_dry_abroad_h: Dry months abroad, from rain gauges
wn_dry_abroad_p: Outside the US, Milpa now knows which months leave nearly every drop of water to you, from rain-gauge records for 1991 to 2020. In those months the Calendar marks the stretch and its month view says so, and your phone’s reminders and the calendar file carry it. Home, the Plan card, Answers and the climate card say the same, and a city’s page shows the months under Summer and rain. How much rain falls each month stays a US-only figure: abroad, the gauge records missed local weather stations by too much in some mountain cities.
wn_ease_counts_h: Counts that add up, Spanish from the first screen, and a week that says one thing
wn_ease_counts_p: A plant team’s plan now says how many plants its layout places; it used to count the kinds. A phone set to Spanish opens Milpa in Spanish, with the switch to English on Home. The Calendar no longer lists a spring sowing as still open beside its fall sowing, a passed indoor start says so instead of rolling a year ahead, “Log the frost” lands on the Log’s frost card, and a raised bed’s depth is asked in your own units.
wn_ease_path_h: A diary with no account, and an easier path through the app
wn_ease_path_p: Your Log no longer needs an account: plant, log a frost or a note, and it stays on this device, then comes with you if you sign in later. Answers finds dates for any town or address, even one that isn’t on our list of cities, and the Plan keeps your place the moment you set it. Home and the Calendar now agree on what to do this week, with a frost two weeks out at the top. Adding a bed fits a phone screen, every plant team has its own Use this team button, a planned bed opens on its plan, and if you know your own frost dates you can enter them right under your place on the Plan.
wn_es_privacy_p: The privacy page reads in Spanish too. The English stays the version that counts, one tap away.
wn_find_indexes_h: Find a plant, a rule or a frost place
wn_find_indexes_p: The site’s long lists open with a search box and show only their first few entries. That covers the plants, the rules, the frost places and their countries, a country’s cities, and the numbers we’re less sure of. Type a few letters, or tap Show 12 more. The plants are compact cards, two across on a phone. In the app, the seed box finds a crop by name instead of a long dropdown, and a plant card with many rules shows five and folds the rest.
wn_first_frost_warmth_h: Your own first frost, where frost is rare
wn_first_frost_warmth_p: Where frost is rare and you gave only your own first frost date, your plans still follow each month’s warmth. Frost-tender crops are sown in time to finish before your date, and their picking ends on it. Since you gave no last frost, they also wait out the cooler months after your date before they’re sown again. Hardy crops keep their months, and the Calendar marks the date as yours.
wn_first_screen_p: On a phone, the landing paints its first screen before the rest of the app has loaded, so it appears about twice as fast, in English and in Spanish.
wn_first_step_h: The front page starts with your planting dates
wn_first_step_p: Type your town or ZIP code on the front page and you go straight to your planting dates. Further down, the evidence opens with a pair of watering answers: one the studies back, and one old tip they rule out.
wn_frost_free_h: Sowing dates where frost is rare
wn_frost_free_p: Where a typical year has no frost, as in Brisbane, Darwin and Miami, the app had no date to count from, so it gave none. Now each crop’s months follow the warmth of each month. The Calendar sows tomatoes, lettuce and the rest in the months they grow well in, Answers says whether a crop can go in this month, and Home names what is in season now. The temperature ranges come from one extension table, so the months are a good hunch to start from. A frost-free place’s page lists what to sow when, and the Can I still sow this? tool names what is in season this month.
wn_frost_gate_h: Frost words only where frost can come
wn_frost_gate_p: Where even the coldest month’s nights stay too warm for frost, as in Singapore, Mumbai or Lima, the pages and the app no longer warn about frost in valleys and hills, and the Log no longer asks you to log frosts. Where a place’s temperatures aren’t shown, What grows here no longer counts a warm-weather crop as fitting, since it can’t check.
wn_frost_inland_h: Frost inland, and a Log that knows one
wn_frost_inland_p: Where the weather model calls frost rare, its pages and the app now say that inland, in valleys and in hills, frost can still come in most winters. In the Log, a note that says frost offers to be logged as one.
wn_frost_menu_h: Frost dates in the Learn menu
wn_frost_menu_p: Frost dates and growing weather is now in the Learn menu at the top of every page, and in the Learn sheet on a phone, two taps from anywhere. The Tools list at the foot of each page now offers Can I still sow this?, and How Milpa compares sits under About.
wn_frost_pick_h: Keep a covered crop going after the first frost
wn_frost_pick_p: When the Log offers to mark the tender crops ended by frost, each crop has its own tick. Untick one you’re keeping going under a cover, and the same tap ends the rest. The next-season plan names a plant family the way the Plan does, the soil card writes every date the same way, and the bars on the coverage map’s cards are easier to tell apart.
wn_grows_here_p: Milpa now sorts every plant it knows for your place: what fits, what needs a little care, and what won’t grow there, each with its reason. It’s on the Answers page under your climate, on each city’s frost page, and on Home when you’re just starting. In Design it yourself, a plant your winters or season can’t carry says so on its row, and you can still add it.
wn_hardy_windows_h: Cabbage, kale and lettuce get their own planting window
wn_hardy_windows_p: A crop that stands a light freeze has until it can still ripen before the first night of about 28 °F (-2 °C), the first hard freeze, which often comes a week or two after the first frost. So in a mild autumn the Calendar, the Plan and Answers keep cabbage, kale, lettuce and their kin open longer, where every crop’s window used to close at the first frost. Cauliflower keeps the first frost, since its head can’t take one. And a bed the Plan keeps for spring names the crop that holds the team back.
wn_home_almanac_p: Home is a page about your own garden. It shows the day and the season, your latest photo, a note on this week, what’s ready to pick, and a chart of where you are in the year.
wn_how_sure_h: How sure is each frost date
wn_how_sure_p: Each city page outside the US now says where its frost dates come from and how sure that kind of source is. One coverage map shows where every listed city’s frost dates come from, and you can narrow it to one country or one source.
wn_large_text_h: Easier to read on a phone
wn_large_text_p: Every page on this site fits a phone at twice the usual text size without scrolling sideways. The Plan’s labels are easier to read in the autumn and winter colors, and the landing’s headline no longer jumps when its font arrives.
wn_lists_app_h: Long lists fold in the app too
wn_lists_app_p: The Calendar’s busy months and weeks, the Plan’s other teams, the seed box, the shopping list and the Log’s layout warnings now show their first few and fold the rest. On the site, the folklore claims gain a search box and the guides fold each long shelf. Small buttons got bigger along the way, and nothing that folds is hidden: a tap shows it.
wn_lists_fit_p: A long list no longer runs down the whole page on a phone. A rule’s plants, a city’s list of what grows there and the Can I still sow this? tool open with how many there are, show the first eight of each group and keep the rest a tap away; tap a group’s count to see only that group. Where frost is rare, a city’s list of what to sow when is a chart of the twelve months, with this month shaded, a switch for what goes in now, and a crop’s kinds a tap away. Every name is still on the page.
wn_log_find_h: Find your way around the Log: by year, bed and kind
wn_log_find_p: The Log’s diary now has a heading for each year, with how many entries it holds. A line above it says which season you’re growing, which you’re planning and which are behind you, and each year in it takes you to that part of the diary. Every entry names its bed, or the whole garden, and what kind it is, and a row of buttons narrows the diary to one bed, one kind, or both. With more than one garden open, the diary, the editor and Undo say which garden an entry belongs to. A planting dated in the future is shown so you can fix the date or keep it.
wn_log_line_h: Say what happened in one line, and the entry is filled in for you
wn_log_line_p: Type or speak a plain sentence into the Log, like “frost last night”, and tap Log it. It also reads “planted 12 tomatoes in bed 3” and “aphids on the kale”: the Log turns the line, on your phone, into the entry it means, a planting, a frost or a problem on a plant, and shows it back to you to check or change before anything is saved. The reading happens on your device: no service sees your words, and nothing is sent anywhere. A sentence it can’t read is kept as the note you wrote, so nothing is ever guessed. It works in English and Spanish, and with your keyboard’s voice typing.
wn_log_review_h: Your season review, from the Log
wn_log_review_p: The Log now has a standing Season in review link under its title, so the review is one tap from your diary as well as from Home. And Import under More now opens the paste box and says what to do, instead of seeming to do nothing.
wn_log_trust_h: A Log you can trust: the right year, and every entry can be changed
wn_log_trust_p: A frost or a hot spell you log goes under the year of its date, from the Calendar too, even while you plan next year’s garden. The Calendar opens on the month you’re in. Each entry on the Log shows its year, and the Edit button beside it lets you change it or delete it, with Undo if you change your mind. A date in the future is refused. Entries that went under the wrong year before this change have moved to their own year, and anything dated in the future is shown to you to fix, delete or keep.
wn_many_doors_h: Doors for the whole season on the front page
wn_many_doors_p: The front page groups its doors by when you need them: before you plant, while it grows, keeping track, and a tip you’ve heard. Each door says what it gives you, and three are new. “What can I plant now?” shows what can go in this week where you live, and what has time to finish before the first frost. “Something wrong in the garden?” matches what you see to its likely cause, from rules a person has checked against their sources. “Keep a garden diary” opens the Log, kept on your device with no account needed.
wn_move_house_h: Moving house? Start a new garden
wn_move_house_p: A free account keeps one garden open at a time. When you pick a new place far from your garden on the Plan’s Where step, it offers “Start a new garden here”: your old garden closes and is kept whole and read-only under Closed gardens on the Log, ready to reopen whenever you like.
wn_names_p: A variety’s card carries the variety’s own name: bok choy’s card reads “Bok choy” instead of “Turnip”. A city that shares its name with others says its country, like Córdoba, Spain, and the Why page’s list says that a tap opens a rule’s whole page.
wn_nearer_station_h: A nearer weather station, named where its frosts end sooner
wn_nearer_station_p: In a few cities, Milpa plans frost dates by a frostier weather station farther out. Where a station nearer the city records its last frost weeks sooner, or none at all, the city’s frost page, your climate card and Answers now name that station and its record, and your plans still go by the frostier one. The coverage map also shows, in a lighter shade, everywhere Milpa answers from the weather model, out to 160 km from its squares, and a country with a frost page now links straight to it, from the map and from the list of countries beneath it.
wn_next_season_h: Your season review plans for the right season
wn_next_season_p: If a season stayed open past its year, the season review now plans for the coming one, as the Log does. Plant teams you chose for a season that never started now move to the coming one too. A soil card that opened before your saved soil had loaded can no longer save its blank answers over it. And the app now clears out the old copies each update left on your phone, so it takes up less room.
wn_notices_h: Reminders that say more with less
wn_notices_p: Milpa’s reminders come as one summary a week, on the day you pick: “Your week”, with the jobs grouped across all your beds. A heads-up comes only on the days that can’t wait: a frost date, a hot or dry stretch starting, a last call to sow. Through a hot or dry stretch, “Your week” reminds you to check your beds each week. The Calendar’s week opens with the same summary, and your calendar app’s alarms ring at most once a day.
wn_one_season_h: Home, the Log and the planner agree on next season
wn_one_season_p: If a season stayed open past its year, Home and the planner could name one already over. Now they name the coming season, as the Log does, and the plant teams you plan for it are there when you start it. A garden placed by a pin in Australia or the UK now gets its own country’s soil-test help. And a few smaller things: milpa.garden/web/#/home opens Home instead of a page saying it can’t be found, the Log’s filter row fades at its edge while more filters wait off-screen and no longer offers a bed with nothing in it, and on a phone the Edit ground button no longer sits on a bed’s name.
wn_own_frost_p: You can enter your own frost dates on the Calendar’s climate card. Your Calendar, your planting dates and Answers then go by your dates, and the card shows the general estimate beside them. Where the dates come from a weather model, the card also says plainly that a model can run weeks warm in hills and inland valleys.
wn_phone_frame_h: A tidier frame on a phone
wn_phone_frame_p: On a phone, the footer folds into groups you open. The Learn tab opens a short sheet of its own: search, the reading pages, and a row to check our work. On a computer, Plants sits under Learn.
wn_reach_us_p: About, For educators and the foot of every page give an email address. Every rule and folklore page has a “Report a problem with this claim” link, and a new page lists every source we read. About also has a note from the maintainer.
wn_rest_order_h: The Plan reads your bed’s rotation, and a season ends in fewer taps
wn_rest_order_p: After a season of beans and squash, the Plan stops leading that bed with a team that brings them back. Those teams come after the others, and a line names the plant families that grew there too recently. Once your first fall frost has passed, the Log marks the tender crops still in the ground as ended by frost in one tap, on the day you logged the frost, or else on your usual first frost date. When a bed’s plants come out on the same day, the Calendar shows one line for each crop. A screen reader now reaches each team card’s Use and Compare buttons on its own, and the Calendar’s days from the months on either side are easier to read.
wn_soil_card_lines_h: The soil card reads more easily
wn_soil_card_lines_p: On the soil card, the advice on finding a lab now gives each point its own line, and where it sends you to the international standard for testing labs it names it, ISO/IEC 17025, so you can ask a lab about it. In the US it asks your lab for the pH in water too. The boxes for a lab report now have their names above them, and the privacy page says you can remove a soil reading and what stays behind. Weather stations abroad show their initials in capitals. In Spanish, the app now says frost comes in most winters, as the site does.
wn_soil_labs_h: Soil tests that fit your country, and a pH reading you can remove
wn_soil_labs_p: A garden with an Australian or UK address now gets that country’s own route to a soil test. The soil card names a lab accredited by NATA or UKAS and, in the UK, the RHS’s soil analysis service. In countries without a card of their own, it says how to find a lab you can trust and what its report should say about your pH, and when we read the pages behind that advice. A lime or sulfur rate printed on your lab report is the one to use, however your lab worked it out. A pH reading saved by mistake can be removed, with Undo. When the soil card can’t check a lab pH, Home and the Log ask for what it needs, which pH your lab gave or a pH in water. The card writes dates the way the rest of the app does, follows your units for the ribbon test and mound heights, and takes a report that grades nutrients on another scale or gives organic carbon instead of organic matter.
wn_soil_world_h: Soil tests that work wherever you garden
wn_soil_world_p: Labs measure soil pH in more than one way, and the pH ranges in Milpa are all written for a pH measured in water. So when you enter a lab’s pH on the soil card, it asks which pH your report gives. A pH in water is checked against your plants. A pH in calcium chloride or another salt solution is saved and shown with how it was measured, and no plant is checked against it, because the gap between the two changes from one soil to the next. A lab pH you saved before this change waits for your answer, and a home kit reading is checked just as it was. The soil cautions read in Spanish in the Spanish app, the soil-test guide’s title and opening and the soil card’s ladder drop their prices, and logging compost leaves your pH reading standing.
wn_sourced_numbers_p: Hundreds more plant numbers now name their source. You can open it from the plant card. Reading those pages changed some numbers. Climbing peas top out lower, fennel, fava and kohlrabi go in closer together, and corn, dill and tomatillo are ready sooner. A variety’s card now shows the source for that variety’s own numbers, and how sure we are of them. Before, it showed the whole plant’s.
wn_south_colours_h: Your own season’s colors, south of the equator
wn_south_colours_p: Milpa’s colors change with the seasons, but south of the equator they waited for you to place a garden, so a first visit from Sydney or Santiago in October met autumn’s colors in your spring. Looking up your ZIP code or town on Answers, on Can I still sow this? or on the frost odds now sets them too. A garden you’ve placed always has the last word.
wn_south_crops_h: New crops for hot summers and southern gardens
wn_south_crops_p: Milpa now knows chicory and radicchio, chickpea, lentil, quinoa, Malabar spinach, New Zealand spinach, luffa, roselle, yardlong bean, mizuna and Florence fennel. Most join the plant teams that suit them, and you can add any of them in Design it yourself. Summer greens, a new team, keeps giving leaves through the heat that sends lettuce and spinach to seed, and What grows here names those greens wherever that happens. The summer legume break, also new, rests a bed with cowpeas through the hot months, ahead of your cool-season crops. Onions now get the day-length type for your latitude, north or south. In Spanish, plants also go by the names used around the Río de la Plata and in Chile, like poroto, choclo, zapallo and betarraga.
wn_sow_by_day_h: Where frost is rare, the last day to sow
wn_sow_by_day_p: Where frost is rare, a crop’s sowing window ends on the last day a sowing can still ripen in the warm months, and that’s usually partway through a month. The app and the site now name that day (“from March to October 11”), and the month charts fill the last month only up to it.
wn_sow_dates_p: Peas, lettuce and radish are hardy crops, so the Calendar now opens their spring sowing about a week earlier. Parsnip and parsley go the other way, a week later. Each change follows an extension planting guide a person read, and the plant pages now show that source.
wn_spanish_site_h: Every page of the site in Spanish
wn_spanish_site_p: What we don’t know, the page for educators and the comparison with other planners read in Spanish too, so every page of the site has a Spanish version. As on every Spanish page, the English is the version that counts.
wn_station_dates_h: Frost dates abroad from a weather station’s own record
wn_station_dates_p: Outside the US, where a weather station with {min} or more years of daily records stands near your garden, its own frost dates now set your plan in place of the weather model’s, and Milpa names the station. That reaches {places} of the cities Milpa knows by name, Melbourne, Paris and Toronto among them, and where a city has a frost page, it shows the station’s dates with NOAA’s citation. The weather model’s dates stay beside them, so you can compare.
wn_station_frost_h: Frost words abroad from a weather station’s own record
wn_station_frost_p: Outside the US, where a weather station with at least ten winters on record stands near your garden, Milpa now goes by how many of those winters brought frost: rare, some winters or most winters. Riyadh’s frost turns out to be rare and Amritsar’s comes in some winters, so their frost words and their planting windows follow. Frost dates still come from the weather model, and the climate card names the station and how far away it is.
wn_stations_h: Frost dates from a station nearer you
wn_stations_p: Each part of the US now reads the weather station nearest where its gardens are. It used to read the one nearest the middle of its square on the map, which could be a mountain while the gardens sat in the valley. Where one station couldn’t speak for everyone, there are two. About a quarter of US ZIP codes read a nearer station. In Fort Collins, Colorado, the last spring frost moved from May 21, a mountain station’s date, to May 2, the town’s own. Station pages you may have saved still open: a page whose station retired takes you to its neighbor’s.
wn_still_time_h: Still time until the window closes
wn_still_time_p: A planting job whose day has passed no longer reads “Late by 280 days” while its window is still open. The Calendar, the bed card and Home now agree: there’s still time, and in the window’s last two weeks the job says the day it closes (“Still time, until Oct 26”). A trellis or other support follows its plant team’s window.
wn_summer_heat_h: Lettuce and spinach, timed around the hot months
wn_summer_heat_p: Lettuce and spinach run to seed when they come ready in hot, long days. Milpa now knows each month’s normal daytime high for every US weather station and every other place it covers worldwide, so the Calendar skips the re-sowings that would come ready in those months and starts them again for fall. The Plan card names the months, the climate card shows the summer’s daytime high, and Home, the Log, Answers and the “Can I still sow this?” tool say so too.
wn_team_jobs_p: A plant team’s planting job says which of its crops can go in earlier. Teams of cold-hardy crops, like cabbage with herbs, are dated weeks before your last frost, and corn gets a sowing date from your frost dates and an approximate picking window.
wn_tell_us_h: A date wrong for your garden? Tell us in one tap
wn_tell_us_p: Under your frost dates on the Calendar and on Answers, “Wrong for your garden? Tell us” opens an email to us in your own mail app, with the dates you see and where they come from already written in. From Answers it also carries the ZIP code or town you gave there, if any; from the Calendar, no address. Nothing is sent until you send it.
wn_tender_end_h: Acorn squash, pot crops, and picking that ends at frost
wn_tender_end_p: Acorn squash has an entry of its own, and a crop with a sourced pot size counts as a pot crop. A frost-tender crop’s picking window ends at your usual first fall frost, on Home and the Calendar alike, and more crops have their Spanish names.
wn_unfit_team_h: A plant team that outgrows its bed
wn_unfit_team_p: When a plant team no longer fits the bed it’s saved on, the Calendar, Home and your bed’s card stop giving it dates. One grayed note takes their place, with what the team needs, what the bed has and a smaller version that fits, and a way to the Plan to switch.
wn_units_frost_h: Your own units from the first page
wn_units_frost_p: Milpa now starts in the units your browser is set up for: meters and °C almost everywhere, inches and °F in the US. And where frost comes in some winters, as in Melbourne, the pages and the app now say so, with the day a frost-tender crop waits for.
wn_verdicts_p: Each folklore page opens with its verdict, and a contested one says whether nothing supports it or the evidence points both ways. A rule whose sources no person has read says so beside its grade.
wn_very_tender_h: Tomatoes and peppers wait for warm days
wn_very_tender_p: Tomato, pepper, eggplant, the melons, pumpkin and winter squash are now marked very tender. Frost kills them and cool days stunt them, so the Calendar and the planting dates wait past your last frost to set them out, until the days stay warm. Their seeds still start indoors on the same day, and a plant team’s planting job says which of its crops wait.
wn_walk_fixes_h: Truer dates and words, wherever you garden
wn_walk_fixes_p: Where frost is rare, a bed is sown from the day you plan it. Wherever you garden, a plan made after its planting day counts its harvest from the day it could still go in, never from a day already past. Four-digit postcodes find your town on the Plan, the bed cards count a crop you have only planned as planned, and the last day of a picking window says the picking ends. On a station’s page where frost is rare, the month chart’s key names all three ways a month can read, and the page says which crops it leaves out and why.
wn_warm_fruit_h: Citrus, avocado and more warm-climate fruit
wn_warm_fruit_p: Milpa now knows lemon, sweet orange, mandarin, Tahitian lime, avocado, mango, banana, passionfruit, olive, pomegranate, feijoa and kiwifruit. Each says which zones it grows in and how it takes frost, and What grows here puts it on your fruit shelf where your winters suit it. Pomegranate and feijoa can now be the tree in the fruit tree ring, and kiwifruit the vine on the kiwi arbor, planted as a male and a female. And where a plant is flagged as a weed somewhere, like the olive in South Australia or passionfruit in Florida, its page, its answer and its row in Design it yourself now say so.
wn_warmth_check_h: Where summers stay cool, warm crops come with a heads-up
wn_warmth_check_p: A frost-free season isn’t always a warm one. Glasgow has more than six months between frosts, but no month there averages the 18 °C (65 °F) or so that okra, tomatoes and peppers grow in. Where frost sets your season and too few months are warm enough for a crop, What grows here now lists it as fitting with care, and the Calendar, your bed’s card and its plant team say why: no month is warm enough, or only July and August are. They suggest cover, an early start or a quick variety. Planting dates stay as they were. Where no month is warm enough, the Calendar no longer promises a picking date, and where only a few are, that date is marked approximate. Later in the season, once a new planting would ripen in months cooler than a warm crop likes, its planting job and your bed’s card say so, even while there’s still time before the frost: in Santiago, tomatoes from January 30. The site’s Can I still sow this? tool now says the same beside each crop. Where frost is rare and you’ve given your own last frost date, your plans still follow each month’s warmth, and only frost-tender crops wait for your date. And where we can’t check a place’s monthly temperatures, What grows here no longer counts luffa, basil and other warm crops with no temperature range on record as fitting.
wn_water_h: Watering, for your place and your beds
wn_water_p: A bed now says whether rain reaches it: open sky, under a roof, or indoors, and a roofed or indoor bed is told that all of its water comes from you. In the months something grows, the Calendar marks the stretches that usually run hot enough to water daily or every other day, and the ones whose rain leaves nearly every drop to you, with each month’s normal rain beside what a growing garden needs in a week. Your phone’s reminders and the calendar file carry them. The Plan card, Home, the climate card, Answers and the place pages that carry rain records say the same, and the watering guide explains it.
wn_which_square_h: Frost dates from the weather square on your own ground
wn_which_square_p: Outside the US, Milpa reads a weather model in squares about 25 km across. Where the squares near you stand at very different heights, your garden now reads the one whose ground is closest to your town’s height, so Viña del Mar reads its own coast and Porto’s last frost comes about three weeks sooner. A square that is mostly sea or lake gives way to the nearest square on land when that one stands at your height, so Sousse now says frost comes in some winters. Height only picks the square and never changes a temperature, and the climate card says which square it read and why.
wn_windows_p: When a planting job’s day has passed but its window is still open, the Calendar says “Still time, until Aug 6” instead of counting the days late. It turns late only in the window’s last two weeks. A team’s window closes on the same day on the Calendar and on its bed’s card, and a close that falls next year names its year.
wn_world_frost_h: Frost dates for cities around the world
wn_world_frost_p: Every city of a million people or more outside the US has a frost page, in English and Spanish. Each Spanish page goes by the city’s Spanish name where it has one. Every page says when the last spring frost usually comes, how late it can be in a bad year, and the odds of an early fall freeze. Each page reads its own country’s weather data, and the frost tools take a city’s name as well as a ZIP code.
wn_world_stations_h: Summer temperatures from weather stations abroad
wn_world_stations_p: Outside the US, a town with a weather station of its own now reads that station’s monthly highs and lows for 1991 to 2020, the way each US place reads its own. Checked against those stations, the weather model ran cool by day, most of all in the mountains, so it caught only some of the hot months: lettuce and spinach timing and hot-weather watering now follow the station wherever a town has one. Where the model reads a town on higher or lower ground, its months stand and its temperatures are left out. The climate card and each city’s page say which you’re seeing, and the coverage page counts where each reaches.
